bacterial_leaf_blight.verified_information: Bacterial leaf blight is caused by bacteria. Young rice plants may turn yellow and wilt. Older plants can get wet-looking orange stripes that start at the leaf tips. Warm, rainy, windy weather and too much nitrogen fertilizer can make it worse. Use the recommended amount of fertilizer, keep the field draining well, and avoid moving water from sick fields into healthy fields.
bacterial_leaf_blight.source: Rice Research and Development Institute, Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture — Bacterial Leaf Blight

brown_spot.verified_information: Brown spot is a fungus that can travel on rice seeds. It makes brown spots on leaves. The spots may be small, or round with dark edges and lighter centers. It can also damage grains and reduce the harvest. Dry weather, poor soil, and high humidity can make it worse. Use clean, certified seed and follow local advice on soil and crop care.
brown_spot.source: Rice Research and Development Institute, Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture — Brown Spot

Healthy.verified_information: The model did not find one of the problems it knows. This does not prove the plant is healthy. The model may miss early signs, other pests, or problems caused by water or soil. Check the whole plant and nearby plants. Ask an agriculture officer if you are unsure.
Healthy.source: Rice Research and Development Institute, Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture — Diagnosing a rice disease

leaf_blast.verified_information: Rice blast is a fungus. It often makes long, pointed spots on leaves. The spots have brown edges and gray centers. It can also damage stems and seed heads. Wet weather, cool nights, crowded plants, and too much nitrogen can make it worse. Use the recommended amount of fertilizer and ask a local agriculture officer if it spreads.
leaf_blast.source: Rice Research and Development Institute, Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture — Rice Blast

leaf_scald.verified_information: Leaf scald is a fungus that can spread through seed. It often starts at the tip or edge of a leaf. The damaged part has tan and reddish-brown bands, then dries and turns the color of straw. It can also harm the seed head and grains. Use clean, certified seed and ask local agriculture staff for advice.
leaf_scald.source: Rice Research and Development Institute, Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture — Leaf Scald

narrow_brown_spot.verified_information: Narrow brown spot is a fungus. It makes thin brown lines along the leaf veins. The lines may join together and damage larger parts of the leaf. It often gets worse as the rice grows older and can reduce the harvest. Use clean, certified seed and follow local advice on crop care.
narrow_brown_spot.source: Rice Research and Development Institute, Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture — Narrow Brown Leaf Spot

neck_blast.verified_information: Neck blast is rice blast on the narrow part below the seed head. It is caused by a fungus. The neck may rot, and the seed head can fall or produce poorly filled grains. Wet weather, cool nights, crowded plants, and too much nitrogen can make blast worse. This image result is not a confirmed diagnosis; ask an agriculture officer before taking action.
neck_blast.source: Rice Research and Development Institute, Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture — Rice Blast

rice_hispa.verified_information: Rice hispa is an insect, not a disease. The beetle scrapes leaves and leaves pale lines. Its young tunnel inside leaves and make see-through patches. Heavy damage can make leaves dry and white. Check for the insect because other problems can look similar. Avoid too much fertilizer and ask local agriculture staff how to manage the pest.
rice_hispa.source: Lucid Central / IRRI rice pest fact sheet — Hispa

sheath_blight.verified_information: Sheath blight is a fungus. It often starts as spots on the leaf sheath near the water or soil. The spots can grow, with pale centers and brown or orange edges. It can spread to leaves and seed heads. Hot, wet, crowded or shady fields and too much nitrogen can make it worse. Use the recommended amount of fertilizer and ask local agriculture staff if it spreads.
sheath_blight.source: Rice Research and Development Institute, Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture — Sheath Blight

tungro.verified_information: Tungro is a virus disease spread by green leafhoppers. Infected rice may be short, have fewer shoots, and have yellow or orange leaves. The seed heads may be small and the grains may not fill well. Other problems can look similar, so ask an agriculture officer to check the plants and look for leafhoppers before taking action.
tungro.source: International Rice Research Institute — Diagnosis of Common Diseases of Rice (Tungro section)
